title: Villa San Giovanni
topic: Combined and relative pronouns: glielo, che, cui

Two pronouns in a row

When an indirect pronoun meets lo, la, li, le or ne, it changes its vowel: mi → me, ti → te, ci → ce, vi → ve.

Me lo dai? — Sì, te lo do.Will you give it to me? Yes, I'll give it to you.

In the third person, gli and le merge with the direct pronoun into a single word, which works for him, her, them and the formal “you”.

lolalilene
mime lome lame lime leme ne
tite lote late lite lete ne
gli / leglieloglielaglieliglielegliene
cice loce lace lice lece ne
vive love lave live leve ne

The order is the reverse of English: “I tell it to him” becomes “glielo dico”, indirect first, and both pronouns go before the verb.

When attached, they form a single word: dammelo (give it to me), voglio dirglielo (I want to tell him). In the past: te l'ho detto, gliel'ho data.

", "

Che, cui, chi

Che means “who”, “which” and “that”. It never changes, and unlike English, you can never leave it out: “the book I'm reading” is “il libro che leggo”.

Il treno che parte. Il libro che leggo.The train that is leaving. The book (that) I'm reading.

After a preposition, che becomes cui. English often puts the preposition at the end (“the city I live in”); Italian always puts it before cui.

La città in cui vivo. L'amico con cui viaggio.The city I live in. The friend I travel with.
La ragazza di cui ti ho parlato. Il motivo per cui sono qui.The girl I told you about. The reason why I'm here.

Between the article and the noun, cui means “whose”: “il vicino il cui cane abbaia” (the neighbor whose dog barks).

Chi means “whoever, the one who”: “Chi dorme non piglia pesci” (literally: whoever sleeps catches no fish; the early bird catches the worm). And “what” in the sense of “the thing that” is quello che.
